metadata.title: Preparing for Life in a Digital World

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: ICILS 2018 used a two-stage cluster sample: schools were sampled with probability proportional to size (enrolled students), and then 20 students were randomly sampled within each selected school (or all students if fewer than 20). Participation requirements were applied at the school and student levels (85% of selected schools and 85% of selected students within participating schools, or a weighted overall participation rate of 75%), with replacement schools used when needed. The report describes multilevel modeling and scaling/equating procedures, but it does not specify the exact survey weight variable names (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) or replicate-weight methods (e.g., BRR/jackknife). For analysts using ICILS microdata, the appropriate approach is to apply the complex-sample weights provided in the ICILS database to obtain population-representative estimates and correct standard errors under the study’s clustered design.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The report states that plausible value methodology with full conditioning was used to derive summary achievement statistics for CIL and CT, but it does not document a missing-data strategy (e.g., listwise/pairwise deletion or imputation) for the student questionnaire/test variables used in the reported analyses. This is a reporting gap because missingness handling can affect multilevel regression estimates and the stability of cross-country comparisons, especially when combining multiple instruments and rotated modules.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used ICILS 2018 grade 8 (or equivalent) student population, defined as students in grade 8 with average age at least 13.5 years (noting Italy’s assessment occurred at the beginning of the school year, so Italy’s CIL results are reported separately for comparability). Students completed two of five CIL modules via a balanced randomized rotation; CT modules were completed only in countries participating in the CT option (eight countries plus one benchmarking participant). Data were included only where they met IEA technical requirements for scoring reliability and sample participation; replacement schools were used when response-rate guidelines were not met. Teacher questionnaires were completed by a random sample of 15 teachers per school (or all teachers if 20 or fewer), and teacher data were not linkable to individual students.

data.outcome_summary: ICILS 2018 assessed grade 8 students’ computer and information literacy (CIL) and, for participating systems, computational thinking (CT) using computer-based tasks embedded in modules delivered in a “walled garden” environment. The CIL instrument used five 30-minute modules with a balanced randomized rotation (each student completed two modules), and CT used two 25-minute modules in randomized order after CIL and the student questionnaire. Achievement scales were derived using Rasch IRT scaling and plausible value methodology with full conditioning to produce summary statistics on an international metric (CIL and CT each with an international mean of 500 and SD of 100 for equally weighted national samples). The report uses multivariate and multilevel models to explain variation in CIL and CT, incorporating student- and school-level influences and reporting cross-country patterns and subgroup differences. Benchmarks are proficiency levels (CIL Levels 1–4; CT regions) and cross-country comparisons, with attention to sampling participation requirements and technical scoring reliability; however, the report does not provide a missing-data handling protocol for the analytic models.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This document is an IEA/OECD-style large-scale assessment report describing assessment design, scaling, and descriptive/multilevel modeling results rather than training predictive ML models. As a result, there are no ML algorithms to extract, no ML target-variable prediction pipeline, and no ML performance metrics (e.g., accuracy/AUC) to tabulate. The extraction therefore leaves main_findings and confounders_identified empty because the report’s primary contribution is measurement and multilevel explanation of achievement and ICT engagement, not supervised ML prediction.
